headline: AI Boom Leaves 63% More Secrets Dangling on the Internet
subheadline: Nine months of aggressive shipping has made corporate crown jewels easier to steal than a Series A deck.
source_headline: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
body_html:
According to Censys data first shared with Axios, the amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months. Let that sink in: in the time it takes a Series B to close, companies have tripled their surface area for catastrophic data theft. No acquisition, no funding milestone, no pivots required—just raw, unfiltered acceleration toward the kind of security incident that makes compliance officers weep into their spreadsheets and makes lawyers start billing by the nanosecond.

The infrastructure in question isn't theoretical. It's the "sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to"—and here we reach the predictable moment where the Axios headline trails off into ellipsis, because even the source material admits nobody actually knows what comes next. This is the infrastructure supporting the models, the APIs, the vector databases, the fine-tuning pipelines, and whatever else founders are bolting onto their stacks at 2 a.m. because a competitor just closed their Series C. It's the plumbing behind the ChatGPT wrappers and retrieval-augmented generation demos that investors have been throwing money at like slot machines. And it's sitting there, humming quietly on the internet, waiting for someone with moderately competent hacking skills to find it.

The pattern is as old as the startup itself, but velocity has changed. The last time we saw this kind of security-by-neglect was during the cloud migration craze—companies rushing to AWS, leaving S3 buckets open, leaking millions of records, issuing apologies, paying settlements. The lesson learned: when executives are being measured on time-to-market and unit economics, security becomes a future problem. AI infrastructure exposure jumping 63% in nine months isn't a bug—it's a feature of the incentive structure. Move fast. Break things. Hire a CISO later, maybe.

The companies building with AI aren't doing anything wrong, technically speaking. They're following the gospel that has powered venture capital for fifteen years: ship first, apologize second, secure third. Every founder pitching an AI product to investors this quarter is carrying a mental model that says: "Better to ask forgiveness than permission." Better to expose infrastructure than to miss the market window. The only difference now is that the window is nine months wide instead of nine quarters.

What could go wrong? Everything. A compromised training pipeline poisoning model outputs. Stolen proprietary datasets becoming competitive weapons. Authentication credentials exposed in exposed configuration files. Database backups accessible to anyone with a Shodan query. The downstream effects ripple through every customer relying on these AI systems, most of whom have no idea what their vendor's infrastructure looks like or who has access to it. When the breach happens—and it will—the apology will cite "an isolated security misconfiguration" and the company will pay for "comprehensive third-party security audits." The founders will retain their jobs. The investors will retain their pro-rata rights.

This is what the AI boom looks like from the infrastructure layer: not innovation, but proliferation. Not security, but speed. The 63% jump in nine months is less a warning sign than a portrait of the era. Every startup racing to ship AI products is racing to expose their own critical systems because the person who worries about security tomorrow gets outcompeted by the person who doesn't worry today. Censys will keep tracking the exposures. Security researchers will keep finding them. Companies will keep shipping them. And venture capitalists will keep funding it all, because a 63% increase in public-facing infrastructure is just market growth with better metrics.

The real security risk isn't malice. It's confidence.
glossary_definition: An euphemism meaning 'infrastructure we built too fast to secure properly and will pretend to understand during the audit.'
